blocks.content: Course: Rapid Build With Claude Code
When it came time to design SpeedBlip, I had three realistic options: Stitch (Google's AI design tool), Framer AI, and Figma. I tried all three. Here is what I found.

Stitch generates UI from a prompt, but the output is limited to simple layouts with no real interactivity or glassmorphism support. It was good for inspiration - I could see roughly how a dashboard might be arranged - but I could not get anything close to production quality out of it. I used it for five minutes and moved on.

Figma is the industry standard for design systems and high-fidelity prototypes. But for a solo build where I had already locked my brand guidelines in a document, Figma was overkill. I did not need a full design system or handoff files. I needed wireframes that were clear enough to write prompts from.

Framer AI was the right tool for this build. It generates a real, interactive website from a text prompt, and with the brand guidelines already defined, I could get a reasonable landing page and app layout in minutes. The free plan has a 2-page limit - I solved that by putting both the landing page and the app section on one long Framer project and treating them as sections.
